    18	
    19	\section{At a glance}
    20	
    21	\begin{itemize}
    22	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The source applies a decoder--encoder
    23	  identity to every bounded individual-degree polynomial, although the identity
    24	  is guaranteed for encoded polynomials and can fail outside the encoding image.
    25	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} One restricted algebraic identity and one
    26	  probabilistic estimate showing that the constructed measurement assigns
    27	  little state-dependent mass to outcomes outside the encoding image.
    28	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Evaluation of the multilinear
    29	  interpolant is elementary polynomial algebra.  The non-encoding-mass bound
    30	  uses project-specific consistency estimates and Schwartz--Zippel.
    31	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} Multilinear interpolation on the
    32	  Boolean cube, injectivity of the low-degree encoding, measurement
    33	  consistency, and Schwartz--Zippel.  The correction is tracked in
    34	  \ghissue{19}.
    35	\end{itemize}
    36	
    37	\section{Key theorem forms}
    38	
    39	For a word $h\colon\{0,1\}^m\to\mathbb F_q$, let $g_h$ be its multilinear
    40	extension.  Define the chapter's decoder by
    41	\[
    42	  \operatorname{Dec}(g)(y)=g(y),
    43	  \qquad y\in\{0,1\}^m.
    44	\]
    45	Then
    46	\[
    47	  \operatorname{Dec}(g_h)=h
    48	  \quad\text{and}\quad
    49	  \operatorname{Dec}(g_h)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_m(u)=g_h(u).
    50	\]
    51	More generally, the second identity holds for a polynomial outcome $g$ under
    52	the explicit hypothesis that $g$ belongs to the image of the encoding; no
    53	converse is asserted.
    54	
    55	For an arbitrary bounded individual-degree polynomial $g$, the Boolean values
    56	determine its multilinear interpolant, not necessarily $g$ itself.  The
    57	unrestricted identity
    58	\[
    59	  \operatorname{Dec}(g)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_m(u)=g(u)
    60	\]
    61	is therefore false.
    62	
    63	\section{Counterexample and source comparison}
    64	
    65	The low-degree encoding is defined at lines~873--897 of
    66	\path{references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex}.  The general decoder at
    67	lines~917--924 retains evaluations lying in a chosen subset $H$; the extraction
    68	chapter instead specifies at lines~1419--1420 of
    69	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex} that the
    70	decoder returns all evaluations on the Boolean cube.  This is the specialization
    71	$H=\mathbb F_q$, rather than the Boolean-valued shorthand used earlier
    72	\cite[lines~873--924 and 1419--1420]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
    73	
    74	Take $m=1$, $d\geq2$, and a field of characteristic two with more than two
    75	elements.  For $g(x)=x^2$, the Boolean evaluations are $g(0)=0$ and $g(1)=1$.
    76	Consequently the decoder is the word whose multilinear extension is $x$.
    77	For any $u\notin\{0,1\}$ with $u^2\neq u$,
    78	\[
    79	  \operatorname{Dec}(g)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_1(u)=u
    80	  \neq u^2=g(u).
    81	\]
    82	Thus the equality asserted for every $g$ at lines~1483--1492 of the chapter-14
    83	source mirror is false \cite[lines~1483--1492]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  If degrees at
    84	least $q$ are allowed, equality as a function would not by itself prove encoding
    85	membership either, since $x^q$ and $x$ induce the same function on $\mathbb F_q$.
    86	
    87	\section{Required repair}
    88	
    89	The extraction proof must split the marginal measurement into encoding and
    90	non-encoding outcomes.  On encoding outcomes, the restricted identity above
    91	justifies the substitution.  On the complement, the proof must bound
    92	\[
    93	  \sum_{g\ \mathrm{not\ an\ encoding}}
    94	  \langle\widehat\psi,\widehat S_g^W\widehat\psi\rangle.
    95	\]
    96	The blueprint derives an $O(\delta_S)+md/q$ bound from point consistency and
    97	the combined point measurement.  A non-encoding polynomial differs from every
    98	encoded polynomial, so Schwartz--Zippel bounds the probability that their
    99	evaluations coincide.  This estimate is the open reduction; it must be proved
   100	from the paper hypotheses rather than inserted as an extraction hypothesis.
   101	
   102	The printed reindexing at lines~1805--1822 replaces
   103	$g_{\operatorname{Dec}(g_W)}$ by $g_W$, which is the invalid reverse identity
   104	for an arbitrary polynomial outcome.  In the corrected calculation, the
   105	constraint is
   106	$g_h(u)=\operatorname{Dec}(g_W)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_m(u)-a$.
   107	After setting $h'=h+\operatorname{Dec}(g_W)$, the defining evaluation formula
   108	$g_k(u)=k\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_m(u)$ and characteristic two turn
   109	that constraint into $g_{h'}(u)=a$.  Thus this step uses neither decoder
   110	linearity nor the identity $\operatorname{Dec}(g_h)=h$
   111	\cite[lines~1805--1822]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   112	
   113	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
   114	
   115	Definition~\path{def:qld-full-field-decoder} and
   116	Lemmas~\path{lem:qld-decoder-linearity} and
   117	\path{lem:qld-decoder-evaluation} in
   118	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex} state the full-field
   119	decoder, its linearity and inverse, and the evaluation identity restricted to
   120	encoding outcomes.  Lemma~\path{lem:qld-nonencoding-mass-bound}
   121	separately records the estimate on the remaining outcomes.
   122	
   123	The declarations \path{decodeFq_add}, \path{decodeFq_smul}, and
   124	\path{decodeFq_lowDegreeEncoding} in
   125	\path{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Algebra/Decoding.lean} match the three algebraic assertions.
   126	In the same file, \path{IsEncoding} is the equality

   141

   143	
   144	The decoding identity is false for a general polynomial outcome.  Restricting
   145	it to the encoding image is a necessary local correction.  Recovering the

    18	
    19	\section{At a glance}
    20	
    21	\begin{itemize}
    22	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The source quotes a fiberwise consequence
    23	  of a state-dependent quantum linearity theorem, but suppresses two averages
    24	  and a compatibility argument for the auxiliary spaces.
    25	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} One faithful theorem for a single family,
    26	  followed by a finite common-extension construction that makes the auxiliary space
    27	  uniform over the outer parameters.
    28	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Finite direct sums, extensions of
    29	  operators, and squared norms are standard linear algebra.  The imported
    30	  quantum linearity theorem and its state-dependent metric are project-level
    31	  inputs.
    32	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} Theorem~10 of
    33	  \cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}, finite averaging, and extension by the identity
    34	  on orthogonal summands.  This reduction is tracked in
    35	  \ghissue{19}.
    36	\end{itemize}
    37	
    38	\section{Key theorem forms}
    39	
    40	Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let $\rho$ be an arbitrary
    41	density operator on $H$, and let $u\mapsto O^u$ be binary observables on $H$,
    42	indexed by $\mathbb F_2^t$.  The cited theorem assumes the averaged
    43	correlation estimate
    44	\[
    45	  \mathop{\mathbb E}_{u,v}
    46	  \operatorname{Tr}\!\left(O^u O^v O^{u+v}\rho\right) \geq 1-\delta.
    47	\]
    48	It produces an auxiliary space $H'$, a unit vector $\mathrm{anc}\in H'$, and
    49	binary observables $L^u$ on $H\otimes H'$ satisfying, with
    50	$\rho'=\rho\otimes|\mathrm{anc}\rangle\langle\mathrm{anc}|$,
    51	\[
    52	  L^uL^v=L^{u+v}
    53	  \quad\text{for every }u,v.
    54	\]
    55	Moreover,
    56	\[
    57	  \mathop{\mathbb E}_{u}
    58	  \operatorname{Tr}\!\left((L^u-O^u\otimes I_{H'})^\dagger
    59	    (L^u-O^u\otimes I_{H'})\,\rho'\right)\leq\delta.
    60	\]
    61	In particular, $L^0=I$: exact linearity gives $(L^0)^2=L^0$, while an
    62	observable is invertible.
    63	
    64	The chapter needs a parameterized version.  For each pair $(x,z)$ it applies
    65	the theorem to $(r,s)\mapsto O^{x,z,r,s}$.  Since the provider theorem accepts
    66	the actual nonnegative defect on each fiber, no assumption that a fiber defect
    67	is at most one, and no good--bad fiber split, is needed.  One must still
    68	formulate the finite common-extension step that makes the auxiliary space
    69	uniform over $(x,z)$.
    70	
    71	\section{Comparison with the quoted statement}
    72	
    73	Lines~711--725 of
    74	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex} quote the
    75	linearity theorem.  The displayed hypothesis correctly averages over both
    76	group variables.  The displayed conclusion, however, says that the corrected
    77	observable is close for every $u$, whereas Theorem~10 of the cited work gives
    78	closeness only on average over $u$ \cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}.  The quotation
    79	also inserts $\delta\leq1$, which is absent from the provider theorem and would
    80	unnecessarily obstruct applying it with a fiber's actual defect.  The assertion
    81	at the identity follows from exact linearity as above.
    82	
    83	Lines~825--832 construct the family $O^{x,z,r,s}$ and establish approximate
    84	linearity only after averaging over $x,z,r,r',s,s'$.  They then apply the
    85	single-family theorem separately for every $(x,z)$ and state that sufficiently
    86	many zero ancillas avoid a further extension.  The remaining implicit step is
    87	to make the theorem's possibly fiber-dependent auxiliary spaces uniform.
    88	
    89	The finite setting admits a standard repair.  Apply the theorem on each fiber
    90	with its actual defect, choose one finite auxiliary space large enough for all
    91	returned spaces, and embed each returned space so that its unit vector maps to
    92	one fixed vector.  Extend the conjugated observables by the identity on the
    93	orthogonal complement.  The embeddings may depend on the fiber because the
    94	observables do.  Averaging then yields the conclusion used later in the
    95	chapter.  This is an open reduction, not a counterexample to the quoted theorem
    96	or to the source's eventual combined-measurement conclusion.
    97	
    98	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
    99	
   100	Theorem~\path{thm:linearity} and
   101	Remark~\path{rem:linearity-import} in
   102	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex} record respectively the
   103	averaged provider theorem and the common-ancilla obligation for its fiberwise
   104	use.  The relevant material is at lines~98--147 and 149--191 of that chapter.
   105	
   106	The declaration \path{exists_exactly_linear_observables} in
   107	\path{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Combining/Linearity.lean} assumes a nonnegative defect, a
   108	positive semidefinite trace-one operator, binary observables, and the averaged
   109	three-observable correlation.  It returns one finite ancillary space and
   110	normalized ancillary vector for that family, exactly linear binary observables
   111	on the extension, and only the averaged squared-distance bound with the same
   112	defect.  It neither assumes $\delta\leq1$ nor asserts pointwise closeness.  Its
   113	statement therefore matches the provider-faithful blueprint theorem rather
   114	than the strengthened quotation in the QPBT paper.  Its proof remains open,
   115	and no Lean declaration yet supplies the finite common-extension construction
   116	for the family indexed by $(x,z)$.
   117	
   118	Issue~\#19 introduced this discrepancy record for the extraction skeleton;
   119	\ghissue{47} owns the Stage~4.3 proof work consumed downstream.  The chapter-16
   120	extraction declarations consume the concrete \path{GlobalPairWitness}; they
   121	do not assume a new fiberwise linearity hypothesis or a common ancillary space.
   122	
   123	\section{Conclusion}
   124	
   125	The primary discrepancy is a quantifier mismatch in the quotation: the cited
   126	linearity theorem gives average, not pointwise, closeness.  Its use for the
   127	family indexed by $(x,z)$ also requires an explicit finite common-extension
   128	argument.  Both are open formal reductions compatible with the intended
   129	source conclusion.

    18	
    19	\section{At a glance}
    20	
    21	\begin{itemize}
    22	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The extraction proof contains two
    23	  incorrect numerical steps and later suppresses the range projection when
    24	  passing from unitary conjugation to isometry conjugation.
    25	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} A corrected positive-contraction estimate,
    26	  a small-error case split for normalization, and one range-projection transfer
    27	  lemma for a projective measurement family.
    28	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Positivity, contraction inequalities,
    29	  isometry range projections, and norm estimates belong to finite-dimensional
    30	  Hilbert-space algebra.  The state-dependent family distance and register
    31	  placements are project-local.
    32	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} The inequality
    33	  $H^2\geq2H-I$ for a positive contraction, the triangle inequality, and
    34	  $Q=\phi\phi^\dagger$ for an isometry.  The repair is tracked in
    35	  \ghissue{19}.
    36	\end{itemize}
    37	
    38	\section{Key theorem forms}
    39	
    40	Let $H_X$ and $H_Z$ be the positive contractions of the extraction proof, and
    41	let $\vartheta$ be a unit vector such that
    42	\[
    43	  \langle\vartheta,H_W\vartheta\rangle\geq1-\delta/2
    44	  \qquad (W\in\{X,Z\}).
    45	\]
    46	Since $(I-H_W)^2\geq0$,
    47	\[
    48	  H_W^2\geq2H_W-I,
    49	  \qquad
    50	  \langle\vartheta,H_W^2\vartheta\rangle\geq1-\delta.
    51	\]
    52	Also $\lVert(I-H_W)\vartheta\rVert^2\leq\delta$, whence
    53	\[
    54	  \lVert H_X\vartheta-H_Z\vartheta\rVert^2\leq4\delta.
    55	\]
    56	Together with $H_XH_Z$ equal to the EPR projection, these estimates give the
    57	required overlap bound, with constants absorbed into the stated
    58	$O(\sqrt\delta)$ error.
    59	
    60	For the final transfer, let $\phi\colon\mathcal H\to\mathcal K$ be an isometry
    61	and set $Q=\phi\phi^\dagger$.  If $N_h$ is the unitary-conjugated extension of
    62	a measurement operator $M_h$, then the exact identity is
    63	\[
    64	  \phi M_h\phi^\dagger=N_hQ=QN_h,
    65	\]
    66	not merely $N_h$.  Thus comparison of $N_h$ with an ideal projector must be
    67	combined with control of $(I-Q)\Delta$ on the ideal comparison state
    68	$\Delta$.
    69	
    70	\section{Numerical defects in the source proof}
    71	
    72	Lines~1715--1742 of
    73	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}
    74	construct $H_X,H_Z$ and identify $H_XH_Z$ with the EPR projection.  The norm
    75	estimate at lines~1743--1750 gives
    76	$\lVert(I-H_W)\vartheta\rVert\leq\sqrt\delta$.  At lines~1753--1757 the
    77	source substitutes $\delta$ inside the reverse triangle inequality
    78	\cite[lines~1715--1783]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  That replacement is not valid for
    79	small $\delta$.  The desired lower bound on
    80	$\langle H_W^2\rangle$ follows directly from $H_W^2\geq2H_W-I$, as above.
    81	
    82	The triangle inequality yields
    83	\[
    84	  \lVert H_X\vartheta-H_Z\vartheta\rVert\leq2\sqrt\delta,
    85	\]
    86	so its square is at most $4\delta$.  Line~1761 instead bounds that square by
    87	$2\sqrt\delta$ without a stated restriction.  This inequality follows when
    88	$\delta\leq1/4$; for larger error the theorem is made trivial by enlarging the
    89	universal constant.  The same small-error split ensures that the projected
    90	vector defined at lines~1769--1773 is nonzero before it is normalized.  These
    91	are local numerical repairs and do not weaken the extraction conclusion.
    92	
    93	\section{The range-projection obligation}
    94	
    95	Lines~1827--1858 prove state-dependent closeness for the concrete operators
    96	obtained by conjugating the original measurement with the swap unitaries.
    97	Lines~1864--1875 then define isometries by adjoining EPR pairs and applying
    98	those unitaries, and immediately state the corresponding closeness for
    99	$\phi M_h\phi^\dagger$.  The omitted range projection makes this implication
   100	non-definitional \cite[lines~1827--1875]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   101	
   102	Let $\Psi$ be the original state and suppose $\phi\Psi$ is close to the ideal
   103	state $\Delta$.  Since $Q\phi\Psi=\phi\Psi$ and $Q$ is a contraction, the
   104	triangle inequality bounds $(I-Q)\Delta$ by the state-extraction error.  Using
   105	$\phi M_h\phi^\dagger=N_hQ$, split
   106	\[
   107	  (N_hQ-T_h)\Delta
   108	  =(N_h-T_h)\Delta-N_h(I-Q)\Delta,
   109	\]
   110	where $T_h$ is the ideal Pauli projector.  Summing squared norms over $h$
   111	uses projectivity and orthogonality to keep the second term under control.
   112	The same argument is required for each player and each Pauli basis.
   113	
   114	This transfer is an open proof obligation for the next extraction stage.  It

    18	/-- The formalization-only embedding of Boolean coordinates into a field used by

    21	def boolToScalar {K : Type*} [Field K] : Bool → K
    22	  | false => 0
    23	  | true => 1
    24	
    25	/-- The coordinatewise Boolean-cube embedding used by

    27	`04_preliminaries.tex:917-924`. -/
    28	def cubeEmbed {K : Type*} [Field K] {m : ℕ} : Cube m → (Fin m → K) :=
    29	  fun y i => boolToScalar (y i)
    30	
    31	/-- On the Boolean cube, an indicator polynomial evaluates to the corresponding
    32	Kronecker delta.  This is the interpolation observation at paper lines 880-891. -/
    33	private theorem eval_indicatorPoly_cubeEmbed {K : Type*} [Field K] {m : ℕ}
    34	    (y z : Cube m) :
    35	    MvPolynomial.eval (cubeEmbed (K := K) z) (indicatorPoly (K := K) y) =
    36	      if y = z then 1 else 0 := by
    37	  classical
    38	  rw [indicatorPoly, MvPolynomial.eval_prod]
    39	  simp only [apply_ite, MvPolynomial.eval_X, MvPolynomial.eval_sub, map_one]
    40	  have hfactor (i : Fin m) :
    41	      (if y i then cubeEmbed (K := K) z i else 1 - cubeEmbed (K := K) z i) =
    42	        if y i = z i then 1 else 0 := by
    43	    cases hy : y i <;> cases hz : z i <;> simp_all [cubeEmbed, boolToScalar]
    44	  simp_rw [hfactor]
    45	  rw [Fintype.prod_boole]
    46	  split_ifs <;> simp_all [funext_iff]

    48	/-- Evaluating a low-degree encoding at an embedded Boolean point recovers its
    49	coefficient at that point, as stated at paper line 891. -/
    50	private theorem lowDegreeEnc_cubeEmbed {K : Type*} [Field K] {m : ℕ}
    51	    (a : Cube m → K) (z : Cube m) :
    52	    lowDegreeEnc a (cubeEmbed z) = a z := by
    53	  rw [lowDegreeEnc_eq_dotProduct]
    54	  simp [dotProduct, indicatorVec, eval_indicatorPoly_cubeEmbed]

    57	`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:445-455`, paper `04_preliminaries.tex:917-924`. -/
    58	noncomputable def decodeAt {K : Type*} [Field K] [DecidableEq K] {m : ℕ}
    59	    (H : Finset K) (g : (Fin m → K) → K) : Cube m → K :=
    60	  fun y => if g (cubeEmbed y) ∈ H then g (cubeEmbed y) else 0
    61	
    62	/-- Boolean specialization of `def:decoding-map`, blueprint
    63	`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:445-455`, paper `04_preliminaries.tex:917-924`. -/

    83	  decodeAt (Finset.univ : Finset K) (fun x => MvPolynomial.eval x g)
    84

    86	is exactly the multilinear representative reconstructed from its full-field
    87	decoder.  This predicate is used to state the support restriction required by

    94	  lowDegreeEncoding (decodeFqRep g) = g

    97	`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:445-455`, paper `04_preliminaries.tex:917-924`. -/

     5	
     6	This module encodes the Boolean subcube by multilinear indicator polynomials
     7	and packages the resulting low-degree code as honest polynomial representatives.
     8	
     9	## References
    10	
    11	The source-facing nodes are `def:polynomials-degree`,
    12	`def:low-degree-encoding`, and `def:indicator-vector` in
    13	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:321-417`; the paper origin is
    14	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.

    20	open MvPolynomial
    21	
    22	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    23	
    24	/- The Boolean cube indexes the `2^m` qudits in the low-degree encoding. -/
    25	/-- The Boolean cube indexing the `2^m` qudits of the test.  This is the index
    26	type in `def:low-degree-encoding`, blueprint
    27	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:381-401`, paper origin
    28	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.
    29	-/
    30	abbrev Cube (m : ℕ) := Fin m → Bool
    31	
    32	/--
    33	The representative polynomial which is `1` at `y` on the Boolean cube and
    34	zero at the other cube points.  This is the indicator polynomial in
    35	`def:low-degree-encoding` (blueprint lines 381-401; paper
    36	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`).
    37	-/
    38	noncomputable def indicatorPoly {K : Type*} [CommRing K] {m : ℕ} (y : Cube m) :
    39	    MvPolynomial (Fin m) K :=
    40	  ∏ i : Fin m, if y i then X i else (1 - X i)
    41	
    42	/--
    43	The multilinear low-degree encoding of a coefficient string.  Polynomial
    44	representatives are used, as fixed by issue #0004, rather than quotienting by
    45	functional equality.  Blueprint: `def:low-degree-encoding`,
    46	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:381-401`; paper origin:
    47	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.
    48	-/
    49	noncomputable def lowDegreeEncoding {K : Type*} [CommRing K] {m : ℕ}
    50	    (a : Cube m → K) : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K :=
    51	  ∑ y : Cube m, a y • indicatorPoly y
    52	
    53	/- Evaluation shorthand for the representative polynomial in
    54	`def:low-degree-encoding`; it is Lean-only notation. -/
    55	/-- Evaluation shorthand for the low-degree encoding.  Blueprint
    56	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:381-401`, paper origin
    57	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.
    58	-/
    59	noncomputable def lowDegreeEnc {K : Type*} [CommRing K] {m : ℕ}
    60	    (a : Cube m → K) (x : Fin m → K) : K :=
    61	  eval x (lowDegreeEncoding a)
    62	
    63	/--
    64	The indicator vector `ind_m(x)` of `def:indicator-vector`.
    65	Blueprint: `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:403-417`; paper origin:
    66	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.
    67	-/
    68	noncomputable def indicatorVec {K : Type*} [CommRing K] {m : ℕ}
    69	    (x : Fin m → K) : Cube m → K :=

    78	theorem lowDegreeEnc_eq_dotProduct {K : Type*} [CommRing K] {m : ℕ}
    79	    (a : Cube m → K) (x : Fin m → K) :

   932		\label{def:symmetric-equivalents}
   933		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.Placement, MIPStarRE.QPBT.Placement.IsOpposite}
   934		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.ProjectiveSetting.place}

   937		For the remainder of this chapter, as well as in
   938		Chapters~\ref{chap:qpbt-combining} and~\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction}, the
   939		six registers
   940		$\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'\mathsf{A}''\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'\mathsf{B}''$
   941		are partitioned into two ``parties'' in two different ways. The first
   942		scheme takes $\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'$ as one party and
   943		$\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''$ as the other; the second scheme takes
   944		$\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'$ as the first party and
   945		$\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''$ as the second. The \emph{symmetric
   946		equivalents} of a bipartite relation of the form
   947		$M_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \approx_\delta N_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}$
   948		are the three relations
   949		\[
   950			N_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \approx_\delta M_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,,\qquad
   951			M_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'} \approx_\delta N_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''}\,,\qquad
   952			N_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'} \approx_\delta M_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''}\,,
   953		\]
   954		obtained by passing to the second bipartitioning scheme and by
   955		interchanging the first and second party; the symmetric equivalents of
   956		a single-party relation of the form
   957		$M_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \approx N_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}$ are the
   958		same relation on the register pairs $\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''$,
   959		$\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'$ and $\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''$.
   960	\end{definition}

   962	\begin{lemma}[Transfer to symmetric equivalents]
   963		\label{lem:symmetric-equivalents-transfer}
   964		\notready
   965		\uses{def:symmetric-equivalents, def:expanded-state, lem:projective-strategy-setup, def:symmetric-game, def:EPR, def:povm-distance}
   966		Let $\mathcal{S} = (\ket{\psi}, M)$ be the projective strategy under
   967		analysis (Lemma~\ref{lem:projective-strategy-setup} and the convention
   968		following it), assumed symmetric in the sense of
   969		Definition~\ref{def:symmetric-game}: the state $\ket{\psi}$ is
   970		invariant under exchanging registers $\mathsf{A}$ and $\mathsf{B}$, and
   971		both players measure the same operators. Let $\ket{\hat{\psi}}$ be the
   972		expanded state~\eqref{eq:def-psihat}, let
   973		\[
   974			\sigma \colon\;
   975			\mathsf{A} \leftrightarrow \mathsf{B},\quad
   976			\mathsf{A}' \leftrightarrow \mathsf{B}',\quad
   977			\mathsf{A}'' \leftrightarrow \mathsf{B}''\,,
   978			\qquad\qquad
   979			\theta \colon\;
   980			\mathsf{A} \leftrightarrow \mathsf{B},\quad
   981			\mathsf{A}' \leftrightarrow \mathsf{A}''\,,
   982		\]
   983		be the two permutations of the six registers
   984		$\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'\mathsf{A}''\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'\mathsf{B}''$
   985		given by these transpositions, and let $U_\sigma$ and $U_\theta$ be the
   986		corresponding permutation unitaries. Write
   987		$\Pi = \{\Id,\, U_\sigma,\, U_\theta,\, U_\sigma U_\theta\}$ and let
   988		\[
   989			\mathcal{R} = \{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}',\; \mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}'',\;
   990			\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}',\; \mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''\}
   991		\]
   992		be the four register placements of
   993		Definition~\ref{def:symmetric-equivalents}. Then:
   994		\begin{enumerate}

   996			action of $\Pi$ on $\mathcal{R}$ is simply transitive.

   998			$\hilb \ot (\C^q)^{\ot M}$, where $\hilb$ is the common Hilbert

  1001			let $U \in \Pi$. Then
  1002			\[

  1004				\,=\,
  1005				\bigl\| \bigl( (P)_{U(\mathsf{C}\mathsf{C}')} - (Q)_{U(\mathsf{D}\mathsf{D}')} \bigr) \ket{\hat{\psi}} \bigr\|\,,

1	# Blueprint Style Guide & Lessons Learned
     2	
     3	## Core Philosophy
     4	The blueprint is a **bridge between the mathematics and the Lean formalization**. A reader should be able to read a blueprint entry and immediately understand the corresponding Lean declaration. Conversely, someone reading the Lean code should find the blueprint proof sketch faithful to what the code actually does.
     5	
     6	## General Principles
     7	1. **Blueprint ↔ Lean must match.** Every `\lean{X}` tag must correspond to an actual Lean declaration. Every proof sketch must match what the Lean proof actually does — not a hand-wavy version of it.
     8	2. **Standalone.** `blueprint/` and any slides are independent — no cross-references, no shared files. Each has its own macros, its own `references.bib`.
     9	3. **Mathematical language only — zero Lean jargon.** No Lean identifiers in prose (no `selfImprovement_step`, no `PastingLemma.aux`, no `rintro ⟨X, hX⟩`). The `\lean{...}` tag is the link; the body text is standard mathematics. If you can't say it in math, rewrite it.
    10	4. **No filler prose.** Only precise definitions, theorem statements, and proof sketches. No "this is important because..." or "the self-improvement step governs the induction...".
    11	5. **Cite non-trivial things.** Basic definitions don't need citations. Important results and non-obvious definitions should cite the source paper.
    12	6. **Don't invent terminology or notation.** Don't create ad-hoc notation when standard notation exists. Don't name things that the literature doesn't name.
    13	7. **Match Lean's theorem/lemma/def exactly.** If Lean says `theorem X`, use `\begin{theorem}`. If Lean says `lemma X`, use `\begin{lemma}`. `\begin{proposition}` is allowed in blueprint prose when it improves mathematical readability, but still map it to an actual Lean `theorem`/`lemma` declaration via `\lean{...}`. Label prefix: `thm:` for theorem, `lem:` for lemma, `def:` for definition, `prop:` for proposition.
    14	
    15	### Remark On Mathematical Prose
    16	
    17	Blueprint entries should read as mathematical exposition, not as progress
    18	reports. The mathematical argument should determine the order of the prose:
    19	introduce the notation, state the assertion, give the proof or calculation, and
    20	then record Lean references through the usual blueprint tags. Lean declarations,
    21	file paths, and proof-status information should not become the visible structure
    22	of the paragraph. When referring to a source article, cite it bibliographically
    23	rather than relying on an uncited reference to the article.
    24	
    25	Use displayed formulae when the formula benefits from visual separation, and
    26	keep short scalar definitions or elementary inequalities inline when the
    27	sentence reads better that way. As in ordinary mathematical writing, displayed
    28	formulae should be punctuated as part of the sentences in which they occur.
    29	
    30	## Proof Sketches Must Match Lean
    31	This is the most important rule. Every proof in the blueprint must faithfully describe what the Lean proof does:
    32	
    33	- **Reference the actual lemmas used.** If the Lean proof calls `LDT.selfImprovement`, the blueprint proof should say "By Lemma X.Y (self-improvement)..." and list it in `\uses`.
    34	- **Do not use `\cref` or `\Cref`.** The blueprint does not load `cleveref`.
    35	  Spell out the kind of object and use ordinary references, for example
    36	  `Lemma~\ref{lem:self-improvement}` or `Theorem~\ref{thm:main-formal}`.
    37	- **Describe the actual proof structure.** If Lean does induction on a parameter, say so. If Lean uses a specific decomposition, name it.
    38	- **Don't hand-wave where Lean is specific.** "Standard argument" is not acceptable if Lean uses three specific lemmas. Name them.
    39	- **Don't be more specific than Lean.** If Lean uses `simp` to close a goal, a one-line sketch is fine.
    40	- **`\uses` in proofs must be accurate.** Only list what the proof actually uses, not what the statement mentions.
    41	
    42	## Source-Labelled Statements And Conditional Helpers
    43	
    44	If a blueprint theorem, lemma, or proposition carries a source label from the
    45	paper, the linked Lean declaration must state the same theorem, up to faithful
    46	formal encoding of the paper's domain.  Do not use `\lean{...}` and `\leanok`
    47	on the source-labelled statement to point to a conditional helper whose
    48	additional assumptions supply an unproved part of the paper proof.
    49	Changing the Lean statement away from `references/ldt-paper/` is strongly
    50	discouraged unless faithful formal encoding or a documented mathematical
    51	necessity requires it; the blueprint should make any such necessity explicit.
    52	
    53	Boundary hypotheses such as nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
    54	positivity of parameters, and denominator nonvanishing may be faithful when
    55	they express the mathematical domain that the paper leaves implicit.  By
    56	contrast, bridge inputs, residual data, repair hypotheses, producer
    57	assumptions, proof-obligation inputs, or package assumptions are proof debt.
    58	They must not be added to a source-labelled theorem statement.  If such data is
    59	still unproved, the source-labelled Lean theorem should keep the source-shaped
    60	statement and carry a tracked `sorry`, or the missing assertion should appear
    61	as the lowest named internal obligation with a tracked `sorry`.  A separately
    62	named conditional helper should not be introduced as a repair pattern.  If one
    63	already contains substantial proof content, it may remain temporarily only as
    64	quarantine: it needs a paper source, a tracking issue, and a discharge or
    65	deletion plan.  The blueprint should leave the paper theorem unmarked as
    66	proof-complete until the source-faithful Lean statement has a source-faithful
    67	proof.
    68	
    69	If a Lean theorem proves only a restricted version of a source theorem, the
    70	blueprint entry carrying `\leanok` must state that restriction in the theorem
    71	statement itself.  It must not be cited as the unrestricted source theorem.
    72	When the only Lean declaration available for a source label has extra
    73	non-paper assumptions, remove the `\leanok` claim from the source-labelled
    74	entry or move the restricted statement to a separate Lean-only entry.  The
    75	unrestricted paper theorem remains unformalized until a Lean statement with
    76	the source's hypothesis set exists.
    77	
    78	## Notation Consistency
    79	Notation must be **internally consistent** across the entire blueprint and **close to what the Lean code expresses**:
    80	
    81	- **Indices**: 0-indexed where matching `Fin n` in Lean
    82	- **Finite fields / alphabets**: use standard notation for the alphabet $\Sigma$ and finite fields $\mathbb{F}_q$
    83	- **Measurements**: use standard quantum measurement notation (projective measurements, POVMs)
    84	- **Strategies**: quantum strategies for nonlocal games should use standard notation from the literature
    85	- **Expansion**: use standard notation for graph expansion parameters
    86	- **Macros** (in `macros/common.tex`): define project-specific macros and use them consistently
    87	
    88	The original reference controls notation whenever it gives a usable convention.
    89	If the blueprint needs a different symbol, index convention, or name in order to
    90	match Lean, introduce it explicitly and relate it to the paper notation in the
    91	same paragraph.  Do not let a `\lean{...}` tag, a Lean namespace, or a file name
    92	be the only explanation of a changed term.
    93	
    94	When a public Lean declaration is a formalization-only auxiliary lemma, the
    95	blueprint should say so before listing the declaration.  The surrounding prose
    96	should identify the paper theorem, equation, or construction that the auxiliary
    97	lemma supports, and should avoid making the auxiliary name look like a named
    98	result from the source article.
    99	
   100	## What NOT to Put in the Blueprint
   101	- **Lean identifier names in math text.** Write "the self-improvement lemma", never "the `selfImprovement` step". The `\lean{LDT.selfImprovement}` tag handles the linking.
   102	- **Implementation details.** Don't say "bundled as an element of the Euclidean space" or "using `EuclideanSpace.equiv`". Describe the mathematical object.
   103	- **Ad-hoc notation.** Don't invent superscripts or subscripts to distinguish from existing notation. Use standard conventions.
   104	- **Function-call syntax.** Use mathematical notation, not programming notation.
   105	- **Redundant definitions.** If two blueprint definitions describe the same mathematical object, consolidate them. Each definition should introduce genuinely new mathematical content.
   106	- **Lean namespace prefixes in prose.** Don't write "the `LDT.PastingLemma`" — write "the pasting lemma".
   107	
   108	## Banned AI/Software Language (enforced in both blueprint AND Lean code)
   109	The blueprint reads as a **mathematical document**, not software documentation. The following patterns are banned in ALL reader-facing text (section titles, theorem names, proof sketches, remarks, chapter preambles) and in ALL Lean docstrings, comments, and section names:
   110	
   111	### Banned terms → replacements:
   112	| Banned | Use instead |
   113	|--------|------------|
   114	| "Assembly" (as section/chapter title) | "Proof of [theorem]", "Construction", "Composition" |
   115	| "Pipeline" | "reduction", "construction", "proof chain" |
   116	| "Bridge" (as noun for a connection) | "connection", name by mathematical content |
   117	| "Handoff" / "hand off" | "transition", "continuation", or drop entirely |
   118	| "In this blueprint" / "Within this blueprint" | "here", "in what follows", or omit |
   119	| "Honest" (as adjective for rigorous) | "exact", "faithful", "unconditional", "complete" |
   120	| "Glue layer" | "intermediate construction", "connecting results" |
   121	| "Re-export" / "reexport" | "provides", "re-states" |
   122	| "Wiring" / "wire up" | "connecting", "composing", "combining" |
   123	| "Package" (as noun for a data bundle) | "form", "data", "structure" |
   124	| "Sorry-free" | acceptable only in Lean-specific technical context |
   125	
   126	### Additional rules:
   127	- **Section names in Lean**: use mathematical terms (`section QuantumSoundness`, `section SelfImprovement`, `section PastingLemma`), not organizational terms (`section Assembly`, `section Pipeline`).
   128	- **Internal LaTeX labels** (e.g., `\label{ch:soundness}`) are not reader-facing and need not be renamed if doing so would break cross-references. But NEW labels should follow the standard.
   129	- **Definitions that are actually theorems**: if a statement asserts a mathematical fact, it must be `\begin{theorem}`, not `\begin{definition}`. Definitions introduce new objects; theorems prove properties.
   130	
   131	## `\uses` Dependency Guidelines
   132	- **Statement `\uses`**: list only what's needed to *state* the result (typically definitions of the objects involved). Keep minimal — transitive deps are automatic.
   133	- **Proof `\uses`**: list only what the proof *actually calls*. Don't list definitions unless the proof unfolds that definition.
   134	- **Never self-reference**: a proof's `\uses` must NOT include the label of the theorem it proves.
   135	
   136	## Recording Formalization-Only Lemmas
   137	Some Lean lemmas are genuine proof infrastructure rather than named statements
   138	from the original papers. These must be traceable without making the blueprint
   139	look as if the paper stated them.
   140	
   141	- If a declaration directly formalizes a paper or blueprint statement, record
   142	  it as usual with `\lean{...}` on that statement and cite the relevant source.
   143	- If a public declaration is an auxiliary lemma introduced only for the Lean
   144	  proof, make that status explicit. Its Lean docstring should say that it is a
   145	  formalization-only auxiliary lemma and should name the nearby paper equation,
   146	  line range, or blueprint result it supports.
   147	- If such an auxiliary declaration is important enough to be referenced from
   148	  the blueprint, give it a clearly subordinate blueprint node, for example
   149	  `[Formalization support for ...]`, and state in the first sentence that the
   150	  lemma is not a named statement of the paper but isolates a step used in the
   151	  Lean proof.
   152	- Connect auxiliary nodes to the corresponding result from the paper with `\uses{...}` from
   153	  the proof that actually calls them. Do not add them only to silence a sync
   154	  warning; the dependency edge should explain where the auxiliary result is
   155	  used.
   156	- Do not mark an auxiliary node with proof-level `\leanok` unless its Lean proof
   157	  is complete and `#print axioms` has no `sorryAx`. Statement-level `\leanok`
   158	  is acceptable only when the Lean statement is intentionally recorded but the
   159	  proof remains tracked as incomplete.
   160	
   161	## Blueprint Structure
   162	- `content.tex` is a router: `\input{chapter/ch01_intro}` etc.
   163	- Each chapter is a separate file in `chapter/`
   164	- Definitions/theorems numbered within chapters: `\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}[chapter]`
   165	
   166	## Lean Blueprint Macros
   167	- `\lean{Namespace.DeclName}` — links to Lean declaration
   168	- `\leanok` — context-sensitive marker; see "Statement-level vs proof-level `\leanok`" below
   169	- `\uses{label1, label2}` — declares dependency edges for the graph
   170	- `\notready` — marks as not ready for formalization (orange in graph)
   171	- `\mathlibok` — already in Mathlib (dark green in graph; see legend note below)
   172	
   173	### Statement-level vs proof-level `\leanok`
   174	
   175	`\leanok` is context-sensitive for human review and graph interpretation. The same macro is used for two different claims, so reviewers should read it by placement rather than by raw token count.
   176	
   177	**Statement-level `\leanok`.** Place this inside a `theorem`, `lemma`, `proposition`, `corollary`, or `definition` environment, on its own line immediately after `\lean{...}`. It says that the corresponding Lean declaration exists and that its statement matches the blueprint or paper statement. It does **not** say that the Lean proof already exists or is complete. For definitions, this is the only `\leanok` marker.
   178	
   179	**Proof-level `\leanok`.** Place this inside the matching `proof` environment, preferably as the first line after `\begin{proof}`. The canonical current placement is the theorem `thm:commutativity-points` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch08_commutativity.tex:8-19`, where the statement block has `\leanok` immediately after `\lean{...}` and the proof block begins with another `\leanok`. This marker says that the Lean proof is complete and free of unresolved `sorry` or unjustified project-level `axiom` shortcuts. In particular, `#print axioms <decl>` must show no `sorryAx`, and the declaration must satisfy the broader blocker rules in the lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference and [`docs/project_conventions.md`](project_conventions.md).
   180	
   181	A theorem, lemma, proposition, or corollary node is **fully formalized in Lean if and only if it has both markers**: statement-level `\leanok` in the statement block and proof-level `\leanok` in the proof block. Statement-level without proof-level means “the statement has been transcribed and matched, but the proof is not yet certified complete.” Definitions have no proof block, so statement-level `\leanok` alone is enough there.
   182	
   183	Excerpt from `blueprint/src/chapter/ch08_commutativity.tex:8-19`:
   184	
   185	```latex
   186	\begin{theorem}[Commutativity of the point measurements]\label{thm:commutativity-points}
   187	  \lean{MIPStarRE.LDT.CommutativityPoints.commutativityPoints}
   188	  \leanok
   189	  \uses{def:good-strategy, def:approx_delta}
   190	  Let $(\psi,A,B,L)$ be an $(\eps,\delta,\gamma)$-good symmetric strategy.
   191	\end{theorem}
   192	\begin{proof}
   193	  \leanok
   194	  The strategy passes the diagonal lines test with probability $1-\gamma$.
   195	\end{proof}
   196	```
   197	
   198	**Current CI behavior.** The advisory Blueprint ↔ Lean sync check in [`docs/ci-blueprint-sync.md`](ci-blueprint-sync.md) distinguishes the two placements. Only proof-level `\leanok` whose axiom closure contains `sorryAx` (or whose harness output cannot be parsed) is reported as an **error**. Statement-level-only `\leanok` with the same finding is downgraded to a **warning**, because statement-level does not claim proof completeness. Each audit line is annotated with the observed placement so reviewers can tell statement-sync work apart from proof-completion work.
   199	
   200	`leanblueprint` does not use distinct macro names for these two claims, so audits must distinguish them by environment context rather than by raw `\leanok` counts. A future split such as `\leanokstmt` / `\leanokproof` could make that distinction explicit, but that is only a possible later cleanup; the current convention is to keep `\leanok` and rely on placement.
   201	
   202	A recurring historical example is the chapter 4 `Q/X/\widehat X/P` witness
   203	layer.  Once Lean has construction theorems deriving the displayed identities
   204	and estimates from the rank-reduction, sigma-range, positive-Gram, native
   205	spectral-theorem, or rectangular-SVD hypotheses, the corresponding blueprint
   206	entries may carry `\leanok`.  A declaration that merely projects an identity
   207	from an opaque data record is not enough by itself, and a theorem depending on
   208	extra rectangular-SVD data should not be used as evidence for an unconditional
   209	paper statement unless a separate construction supplies that data.
   210	
   211	## Dependency Graph Colors (web)
   212	- **Light green box**: definition with `\lean` + `\leanok` (defined in Lean)
   213	- **Green**: theorem/lemma/proposition/corollary with `\lean` + statement-level `\leanok` (statement matched in Lean)
   214	- **Dark green**: either (i) theorem/lemma/proposition/corollary with both statement-level and proof-level `\leanok` (fully formalized in Lean), or (ii) a `\mathlibok` node
   215	- **Blue**: ready to state/prove (all deps are done)
   216	- **Orange**: `\notready` (needs more blueprint work)
   217	
   218	## Bibliography Workflow
   219	1. Edit `blueprint/src/references.bib` (standalone, AuthorYYYYKeyword keys)
   220	2. Run `texra-blueprint bbl` from the repository root — it regenerates
   221	   `blueprint/src/web.bbl` from the `\cite` keys in the blueprint sources.
   222	   `web.bbl` is not committed (`.gitignore` covers `*.bbl`); every CI job
   223	   that runs the web build regenerates it first, and so must a local run.
   224	3. Run `leanblueprint web` (plasTeX reads `web.bbl`)
   225	4. The PDF build needs no separate step: `leanblueprint pdf` runs bibtex on
   226	   `print.tex` itself, and `print.bbl` never feeds the web build.
   227	5. Citation key format: e.g., `Ji2020MIPStar`, `Natarajan2020Quantum`
   228	6. Paper-gap notes: blueprint prose cites `\cite{gap:<slug>}` (never the raw
   229	   `docs/paper-gaps/<slug>.tex` path); each cited note has a `@techreport`
   230	   entry in `blueprint/src/references.bib` with `type = {Paper-gap note}`,
   231	   whose `note` field carries the published PDF URL as `\url{...}` (the
   232	   alpha style of the PDF build drops `url` fields for techreport entries).
   233	   `texra-blueprint bbl` renders such entries with slug-shaped citation
   234	   labels (e.g. `[issue-906-main-formal-k-bound]`) in the web bibliography,
   235	   while ordinary entries keep alpha labels. Lean docstrings and comments
   236	   keep the repository path form.
   237	
   238	## Stale/Corrupt Aux File Recovery
   239	If LaTeX reports `! File ended while scanning use of \@newl@bel` on startup:
   240	- The `.aux` file was truncated by a previous killed/timed-out run
   241	- Fix: `rm -f blueprint/src/print.aux blueprint/print/print.aux blueprint/print.aux`
   242	- Then rerun latexmk — it rebuilds the aux from scratch cleanly
   243	- `web.bbl` is unaffected: it comes from `texra-blueprint bbl`, not from
   244	  `print.bbl`
   245	
   246	## Build Commands
   247	```bash
   248	leanblueprint pdf     # PDF → blueprint/print/print.pdf
   249	leanblueprint web     # HTML → blueprint/web/
   250	leanblueprint serve   # local server at http://0.0.0.0:8000/
   251	leanblueprint all     # pdf + web + checkdecls
   252	```

1	# Mathematical Language Guidelines
     2	
     3	MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
     4	the formalization with the paper and blueprint.
     5	
     6	This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
     7	naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
     8	`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.
     9	
    10	## Scope
    11	
    12	These guidelines apply to:
    13	
    14	- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
    15	- module docstrings;
    16	- declaration docstrings;
    17	- documentation-visible section comments;
    18	- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
    19	- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
    20	- issue titles and issue bodies;
    21	- PR titles and PR descriptions.
    22	
    23	## Source of Truth
    24	
    25	Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:
    26	
    27	1. `references/ldt-paper/`
    28	2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
    29	3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files
    30	
    31	When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
    32	example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
    33	projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.
    34	
    35	## Reference Notation And Terminology
    36	
    37	The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
    38	reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
    39	docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
    40	without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.
    41	
    42	When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
    43	location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
    44	first applicable location in the following order:
    45	
    46	1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
    47	   differs from the paper;
    48	2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
    49	   family of declarations in that file;
    50	3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
    51	   blueprint;
    52	4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
    53	   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.
    54	
    55	The explanation should say:
    56	
    57	- the notation or term used in the paper;
    58	- the Lean object or name which represents it;
    59	- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
    60	- the scope in which the replacement should be used.
    61	
    62	A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
    63	where future readers can learn it.
    64	
    65	Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
    66	should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
    67	rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.
    68	
    69	## Naming Norm
    70	
    71	Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
    72	conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
    73	assembled.
    74	
    75	Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
    76	`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
    77	uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
    78	such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
    79	clearer phrase.
    80	
    81	This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
    82	Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
    83	blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
    84	mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
    85	number, or implementation history.
    86	
    87	### Concrete examples
    88	
    89	The table below illustrates the naming norm with examples patterned on the
    90	codebase and on names seen during review.  Some entries are existing names;
    91	others are proposed names for future refactors.  The "avoid" column lists
    92	process-shaped names that encode the history of how the formalization was
    93	assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
    94	paper or blueprint would recognize.
    95	
    96	| Avoid (process-shaped)                        | Prefer (mathematical)                     | Rationale                                              |
    97	|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
    98	| `Line130`                                     | `ProjectiveConsistency`                   | Paper Lemma 5.13, not "the line-130 identity"          |
    99	| `Line169`                                     | `CompletionTransport`                     | Paper Lemma 5.16, step that transports completed data  |
   100	| `Step6`                                       | `Orthonormalization`                      | Paper Section 5, the orthonormalization construction   |
   101	| `FinalAssembly`                               | `DiagonalCompletion`                      | Paper Lemma 5.17, constructing a diagonal POVM         |
   102	| `OneShotIneq`                                 | `SelfConsistencyDataProcessing` (or existing module `Preliminaries.SelfConsistency.DataProcessing`)           | Paper's data-processing inequality for self-consistency |
   103	| `PipelineCheck`                               | `ErrorPropagationBound` (proposed)                   | The bound that propagates error through the test       |
   104	| `QxpLayerWrapper`                             | `ProjectivePOVMCompletion` (proposed)                | The construction from round-projectors to POVMs        |
   105	| `RawSpectralTruncation`                       | `SpectralTruncation`                      | The paper's spectral truncation, not an "unwrapped" version |
   106	| `AddInUStep3To5`                              | `AddInUUpperExcessMass` (proposed)                  | Paper Addendum in §U, the upper excess-mass estimate   |
   107	| `AddInUStep12`                                | `AddInUCommutationTail` (proposed)                   | Paper Addendum in §U, the commutation tail estimate    |
   108	
   109	An avoided name is acceptable only when the cited paper itself uses that
   110	phrase as the mathematical name (e.g., a lemma the paper calls "Step 2").
   111	In that case the docstring should cite the paper's phrasing.
   112	
   113	File-split PRs are a common place where this rule matters: new leaves should be
   114	named by the mathematical boundary they isolate, and any public declarations
   115	exposed by the split should be reviewed under the same standard.
   116	
   117	### Shared helpers
   118	
   119	When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
   120	more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
   121	shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
   122	ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
   123	call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.
   124	
   125	Procedure:
   126	
   127	1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   128	   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   129	   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   130	   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   131	   explicit argument.
   132	2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   133	   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   134	   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   135	   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   136	   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
   137	3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   138	   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
   139	4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   140	   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   141	   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   142	   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   143	   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   144	   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
   145	5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   146	   blueprint location it supports.
   147	
   148	### Legacy identifier treatment
   149	
   150	If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
   151	describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
   152	identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
   153	in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.
   154	
   155	Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
   156	public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
   157	shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
   158	blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.
   159	
   160	## Review Checklist
   161	
   162	Reviewers should use this checklist when examining public names and
   163	documentation prose.  Flag any item that fails.
   164	
   165	- [ ] **Naming.**  Do public declaration names, namespace names, module names,
   166	      theorem field names, and docstring prose describe a mathematical object,
   167	      hypothesis, or conclusion?  Or do they encode the history of how the
   168	      formalization was assembled (paper line numbers, workflow steps,
   169	      implementation-phase labels)?
   170	- [ ] **Source alignment.**  For the mathematical content under review, does
   171	      the prose use the terminology in `references/ldt-paper/` or the
   172	      blueprint?  Are process words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`,
   173	      `raw`, `oneShot`, or `liveBlock` used as mathematical terms when the
   174	      source does not use them that way?
   175	- [ ] **Deviation documented.**  If a Lean name or representation differs from
   176	      the paper, is the deviation documented in a declaration docstring,
   177	      module docstring, blueprint paragraph, or `docs/paper-gaps/` note, in
   178	      that order of preference?
   179	- [ ] **Auxiliary lemmas.**  Are formalization-only auxiliary lemmas introduced
   180	      as such, with prose naming the nearby paper equation, theorem, or
   181	      construction they support?
   182	- [ ] **Shared helpers.**  Does the PR introduce a helper that already exists
   183	      (or near-exists) in another chapter-local leaf?  If so, has it been
   184	      consolidated into a common module with a mathematical name?
   185	- [ ] **Legacy IDs.**  If a legacy Lean identifier is mentioned, is the
   186	      mathematical object described in paper terminology?  If an old public
   187	      identifier cannot be renamed yet, is the required migration recorded in
   188	      the issue, PR description, or an audit file?
   189	- [ ] **Pass-through names.**  Does the PR add an empty pass-through
   190	      abbreviation that introduces a second public name without adding
   191	      mathematical content?  Reject it unless it is a documented compatibility
   192	      wrapper preserving paper-facing or blueprint-facing terminology.
   193	
   194	Review-fix PRs touching a surface covered by an active audit should read the
   195	relevant audit before changing names or prose.
   196	
   197	[#1145]: https://github.com/LionSR/MIPStarRE/issues/1145

    79	Notation must be **internally consistent** across the entire blueprint and **close to what the Lean code expresses**:

    94	When a public Lean declaration is a formalization-only auxiliary lemma, the

    96	should identify the paper theorem, equation, or construction that the auxiliary

   100	## What NOT to Put in the Blueprint
   101	- **Lean identifier names in math text.** Write "the self-improvement lemma", never "the `selfImprovement` step". The `\lean{LDT.selfImprovement}` tag handles the linking.
   102	- **Implementation details.** Don't say "bundled as an element of the Euclidean space" or "using `EuclideanSpace.equiv`". Describe the mathematical object.
   103	- **Ad-hoc notation.** Don't invent superscripts or subscripts to distinguish from existing notation. Use standard conventions.
   104	- **Function-call syntax.** Use mathematical notation, not programming notation.
   105	- **Redundant definitions.** If two blueprint definitions describe the same mathematical object, consolidate them. Each definition should introduce genuinely new mathematical content.
   106	- **Lean namespace prefixes in prose.** Don't write "the `LDT.PastingLemma`" — write "the pasting lemma".
   107	
   108	## Banned AI/Software Language (enforced in both blueprint AND Lean code)
   109	The blueprint reads as a **mathematical document**, not software documentation. The following patterns are banned in ALL reader-facing text (section titles, theorem names, proof sketches, remarks, chapter preambles) and in ALL Lean docstrings, comments, and section names:
   110	
   111	### Banned terms → replacements:
   112	| Banned | Use instead |
   113	|--------|------------|
   114	| "Assembly" (as section/chapter title) | "Proof of [theorem]", "Construction", "Composition" |
   115	| "Pipeline" | "reduction", "construction", "proof chain" |
   116	| "Bridge" (as noun for a connection) | "connection", name by mathematical content |
   117	| "Handoff" / "hand off" | "transition", "continuation", or drop entirely |
   118	| "In this blueprint" / "Within this blueprint" | "here", "in what follows", or omit |
   119	| "Honest" (as adjective for rigorous) | "exact", "faithful", "unconditional", "complete" |
   120	| "Glue layer" | "intermediate construction", "connecting results" |
   121	| "Re-export" / "reexport" | "provides", "re-states" |
   122	| "Wiring" / "wire up" | "connecting", "composing", "combining" |
   123	| "Package" (as noun for a data bundle) | "form", "data", "structure" |
   124	| "Sorry-free" | acceptable only in Lean-specific technical context |
   125	
   126	### Additional rules:
   127	- **Section names in Lean**: use mathematical terms (`section QuantumSoundness`, `section SelfImprovement`, `section PastingLemma`), not organizational terms (`section Assembly`, `section Pipeline`).
   128	- **Internal LaTeX labels** (e.g., `\label{ch:soundness}`) are not reader-facing and need not be renamed if doing so would break cross-references. But NEW labels should follow the standard.
   129	- **Definitions that are actually theorems**: if a statement asserts a mathematical fact, it must be `\begin{theorem}`, not `\begin{definition}`. Definitions introduce new objects; theorems prove properties.
   130	
   131	## `\uses` Dependency Guidelines
   132	- **Statement `\uses`**: list only what's needed to *state* the result (typically definitions of the objects involved). Keep minimal — transitive deps are automatic.
   133	- **Proof `\uses`**: list only what the proof *actually calls*. Don't list definitions unless the proof unfolds that definition.
   134	- **Never self-reference**: a proof's `\uses` must NOT include the label of the theorem it proves.

   137	Some Lean lemmas are genuine proof infrastructure rather than named statements
   138	from the original papers. These must be traceable without making the blueprint
   139	look as if the paper stated them.
   140	
   141	- If a declaration directly formalizes a paper or blueprint statement, record
   142	  it as usual with `\lean{...}` on that statement and cite the relevant source.
   143	- If a public declaration is an auxiliary lemma introduced only for the Lean
   144	  proof, make that status explicit. Its Lean docstring should say that it is a
   145	  formalization-only auxiliary lemma and should name the nearby paper equation,
   146	  line range, or blueprint result it supports.
   147	- If such an auxiliary declaration is important enough to be referenced from
   148	  the blueprint, give it a clearly subordinate blueprint node, for example
   149	  `[Formalization support for ...]`, and state in the first sentence that the
   150	  lemma is not a named statement of the paper but isolates a step used in the
   151	  Lean proof.
   152	- Connect auxiliary nodes to the corresponding result from the paper with `\uses{...}` from
   153	  the proof that actually calls them. Do not add them only to silence a sync
   154	  warning; the dependency edge should explain where the auxiliary result is
   155	  used.
   156	- Do not mark an auxiliary node with proof-level `\leanok` unless its Lean proof
   157	  is complete and `#print axioms` has no `sorryAx`. Statement-level `\leanok`
   158	  is acceptable only when the Lean statement is intentionally recorded but the
   159	  proof remains tracked as incomplete.

   161	## Blueprint Structure
   162	- `content.tex` is a router: `\input{chapter/ch01_intro}` etc.
   163	- Each chapter is a separate file in `chapter/`
   164	- Definitions/theorems numbered within chapters: `\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}[chapter]`
   165	
   166	## Lean Blueprint Macros
   167	- `\lean{Namespace.DeclName}` — links to Lean declaration
   168	- `\leanok` — context-sensitive marker; see "Statement-level vs proof-level `\leanok`" below
   169	- `\uses{label1, label2}` — declares dependency edges for the graph
   170	- `\notready` — marks as not ready for formalization (orange in graph)
   171	- `\mathlibok` — already in Mathlib (dark green in graph; see legend note below)
   172	
   173	### Statement-level vs proof-level `\leanok`
   174	
   175	`\leanok` is context-sensitive for human review and graph interpretation. The same macro is used for two different claims, so reviewers should read it by placement rather than by raw token count.
   176	
   177	**Statement-level `\leanok`.** Place this inside a `theorem`, `lemma`, `proposition`, `corollary`, or `definition` environment, on its own line immediately after `\lean{...}`. It says that the corresponding Lean declaration exists and that its statement matches the blueprint or paper statement. It does **not** say that the Lean proof already exists or is complete. For definitions, this is the only `\leanok` marker.
   178	
   179	**Proof-level `\leanok`.** Place this inside the matching `proof` environment, preferably as the first line after `\begin{proof}`. The canonical current placement is the theorem `thm:commutativity-points` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch08_commutativity.tex:8-19`, where the statement block has `\leanok` immediately after `\lean{...}` and the proof block begins with another `\leanok`. This marker says that the Lean proof is complete and free of unresolved `sorry` or unjustified project-level `axiom` shortcuts. In particular, `#print axioms <decl>` must show no `sorryAx`, and the declaration must satisfy the broader blocker rules in the lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference and [`docs/project_conventions.md`](project_conventions.md).
   180	
   181	A theorem, lemma, proposition, or corollary node is **fully formalized in Lean if and only if it has both markers**: statement-level `\leanok` in the statement block and proof-level `\leanok` in the proof block. Statement-level without proof-level means “the statement has been transcribed and matched, but the proof is not yet certified complete.” Definitions have no proof block, so statement-level `\leanok` alone is enough there.

     3	/-!
     4	# Finite-field bases and the fixed binary representation
     5	
     6	The Pauli basis test uses fields of size `2^k` for odd `k`, together with a
     7	chosen self-dual normal basis over `ZMod 2`.  This file constructs such bases
     8	and records the resulting fixed field model for later proofs.
     9	
    10	## References
    11	
    12	The declarations correspond to `def:admissible-size`,
    13	`def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis`, `def:subfields-kappa`, `def:subfield-trace`,
    14	and `def:binary-representation` in
    15	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:182-257` and `298-315`.
    16	Their paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:433-502,653-728`.
    17	-/
    18	
    19	open scoped BigOperators
    20	
    21	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    22	
    23	/-- `IsAdmissibleSize q` is the predicate `q = 2^k` for an odd exponent.
    24	This is `def:admissible-size` in the blueprint
    25	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:210-212`, with paper origin
    26	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:662-667`.
    27	-/
    28	def IsAdmissibleSize (q : ℕ) : Prop := ∃ k : ℕ, Odd k ∧ q = 2 ^ k
    29	
    30	/-- A dual pair of bases for `def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis`, blueprint
    31	`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:241-257`, paper `04_preliminaries.tex:494-496`. -/
    32	def IsDualBasisPair {F K ι : Type*} [CommRing F] [CommRing K] [DecidableEq ι]
    33	    [Algebra F K] (b b' : Module.Basis ι F K) : Prop :=
    34	  ∀ i j, Algebra.trace F K (b i * b' j) = if i = j then 1 else 0
    35	
    36	namespace Basis
    37	
    38	/-- Self-duality in `def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis`, blueprint
    39	`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:241-257`, paper `04_preliminaries.tex:494-497`. -/
    40	def IsSelfDual {F K ι : Type*} [CommRing F] [CommRing K] [DecidableEq ι]
    41	    [Algebra F K] (b : Module.Basis ι F K) : Prop :=
    42	  IsDualBasisPair b b
    43	
    44	/-- Normality in `def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis`, blueprint
    45	`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:241-257`, paper `04_preliminaries.tex:498-502`. The
    46	Frobenius exponent uses the cardinality of the base field. -/
    47	def IsNormal {F K : Type*} [CommSemiring F] [Fintype F] [Field K] [Algebra F K]
    48	    {k : ℕ} (b : Module.Basis (Fin k) F K) : Prop :=
    49	  ∃ α : K, ∀ j, b j = α ^ (Fintype.card F ^ j.1)
    50	
    51	end Basis

    53	/- The characteristic-two self-dual normal-basis construction is carried out
    54	in the group algebra of the finite Galois group.  The transition from a normal
    55	basis to its trace dual is a symmetric unit; odd cardinality makes its square
    56	root unique and symmetric. -/
    57	
    58	section GroupAlgebra
    59	
    60	variable {G : Type*} [CommGroup G]
    61	
    62	/-- The squaring automorphism of a commutative group whose `Nat.card` is odd. -/
    63	private noncomputable def squareMulEquiv (hodd : Odd (Nat.card G)) : G ≃* G :=
    64	  MulEquiv.ofBijective (powMonoidHom 2) hodd.coprime_two_right.pow_left_bijective
    65	
    66	private theorem monoid_algebra_sq_eq_dom_congr (hodd : Odd (Nat.card G))
    67	    (x : MonoidAlgebra (ZMod 2) G) :
    68	    x ^ 2 = MonoidAlgebra.domCongr (ZMod 2) (ZMod 2) (squareMulEquiv hodd) x := by
    69	  letI : CharP (MonoidAlgebra (ZMod 2) G) 2 :=
    70	    charP_of_injective_algebraMap' (ZMod 2) 2
    71	  induction x using MonoidAlgebra.induction_linear with
    72	  | zero => simp
    73	  | add x y hx hy =>
    74	      rw [add_pow_char, hx, hy, map_add]
    75	  | single g r =>
    76	      simp [MonoidAlgebra.single_pow, squareMulEquiv, ZMod.pow_card]
    77	
    78	private theorem monoid_algebra_sq_bijective (hodd : Odd (Nat.card G)) :
    79	    Function.Bijective (fun x : MonoidAlgebra (ZMod 2) G => x ^ 2) := by
    80	  have heq : (fun x : MonoidAlgebra (ZMod 2) G => x ^ 2) =
    81	      MonoidAlgebra.domCongr (ZMod 2) (ZMod 2) (squareMulEquiv hodd) := by
    82	    funext x
    83	    exact monoid_algebra_sq_eq_dom_congr hodd x
    84	  rw [heq]
    85	  exact (MonoidAlgebra.domCongr (ZMod 2) (ZMod 2) (squareMulEquiv hodd)).bijective
    86	
    87	end GroupAlgebra

    98	private theorem normal_basis_trace_dual_apply (σ : G) :
    99	    (IsGalois.normalBasis (ZMod 2) K).traceDual σ =
   100	      σ ((IsGalois.normalBasis (ZMod 2) K).traceDual 1) := by
   101	  classical
   102	  let b := IsGalois.normalBasis (ZMod 2) K
   103	  have hdual : (b.traceDual : G → K) = fun τ => τ (b.traceDual 1) := by
   104	    rw [b.traceDual_eq_iff]
   105	    intro τ υ
   106	    simp only [Algebra.traceForm_apply]
   107	    calc
   108	      Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K (τ (b.traceDual 1) * b υ) =
   109	          Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K
   110	            (τ⁻¹ (τ (b.traceDual 1) * b υ)) := by
   111	              symm
   112	              exact Algebra.trace_eq_of_algEquiv τ⁻¹ _
   113	      _ = Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K (b.traceDual 1 * b (τ⁻¹ * υ)) := by
   114	        congr 2
   115	        rw [map_mul]
   116	        have hτ : τ⁻¹ (τ (b.traceDual 1)) = b.traceDual 1 := by
   117	          change τ.symm (τ (b.traceDual 1)) = b.traceDual 1
   118	          exact τ.symm_apply_apply _
   119	        have hυ : τ⁻¹ (b υ) = b (τ⁻¹ * υ) := by
   120	          calc
   121	            τ⁻¹ (b υ) = τ⁻¹ (υ (b 1)) := by
   122	              rw [IsGalois.normalBasis_apply]
   123	            _ = (τ⁻¹ * υ) (b 1) := rfl
   124	            _ = b (τ⁻¹ * υ) := (IsGalois.normalBasis_apply _).symm
   125	        rw [hτ, hυ]
   126	      _ = if τ⁻¹ * υ = 1 then 1 else 0 := b.trace_traceDual_mul 1 (τ⁻¹ * υ)
   127	      _ = if υ = τ then 1 else 0 := by simp only [inv_mul_eq_one, eq_comm]

  1415	 \subsection{Pulling the $X$ and $Z$ measurements apart}
  1416	\label{sec:separating}
  1417	
  1418	
  1419	Recall the decoding map of the low-degree code defined in \Cref{sec:ld-encoding}. This map takes in a polynomial $g \in \ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$ and returns a string $\coded(g) \in \F_q^{\nqubits}$ consisting of the evaluations of $g$ on the points in the hypercube $\{0,1\}^m$.
  1420	We now use this decoding map to construct a new set of measurement operators out of $\hat{S}$.
  1421	First, we introduce some notation. For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and all degree $d$ polynomials $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ define projectors
  1422	\[ \hat{S}^X_g = \sum_{g_\zpt} \hat{S}_{g,g_\zpt} \quad  \text{and}  \quad \hat{S}^Z_g = \sum_{g_\xpt} \hat{S}_{g_\xpt,g}\;,\]
  1423	where the measurement $\{\hat{S}_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} \}$  is given by \Cref{lem:qld-4-7}.
  1424	
  1425	For all $W \in \{X, Z\}$, $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^{\nqubits}$, and $a \in \F_q$, define the projector
  1426	\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-tauwu}
  1427	 \tau^{W}_{a}(\tilde{u}) = \sum_{h \in \F_q^{\nqubits} \,:\, h \cdot \tilde{u} = a} \tau^W_{h}
  1428	\end{equation}
  1429	where recall that $\tau^W_h$ is the projector corresponding to measuring $(\C^q)^{\otimes \nqubits}$ in the $W$ basis and obtaining $h \in \F_q^\nqubits$ as the outcome. For all $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^\nqubits$ define the projective measurement $\{ \tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a \}_{a \in \F_q}$ by 
  1430		\begin{equation}
  1431		\label{eq:tilde_M}
  1432		\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a =  \sum_{g} \hat{S}^W_g \otimes \tau_{(\coded(g) \cdot \tilde{u}) - a}^W(\tilde{u})\;.
  1433		\end{equation}
  1434		If $\hat{S}^W_g$ is viewed as an operator acting on registers $\alice \alice'$ (resp. $\bob \bob'$) then we view $\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a$ as an operator acting on registers $\alice \alice' \alice''$ (resp. $\bob \bob' \bob''$). (When necessary we will indicate via subscripts which registers the operators are acting on.)
  1435	The $\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a$ are projective because the $\hat{S}^W_g$ and $\tau^W$ operators are projective.
  1436	
  1437	
  1438		For all $j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$ define the observable
  1439		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-tildewj}
  1440			\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) = \sum_a (-1)^{\tr(e_j a)} \, \tilde{M}_a^{W,\tilde{u}} \;,
  1441		\end{equation}
  1442		where $\{e_j\}_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}}$ denotes the self-dual basis for $\F_q$ over $\F_2$ specified in \Cref{sec:subfields}. Let $\tau^W$ be the generalized Pauli observable defined in Section~\ref{sec:generalized-pauli}. Observe that
  1443		\begin{align*}
  1444		\Big ( \sum_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} (-1)^{\tr(e_j (\coded(g_W) \cdot \tilde{u}))} \hat{S}_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} \Big ) \otimes \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u})
  1445		&= \sum_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} \sum_h (-1)^{\tr(e_j (\coded(g_W) \cdot \tilde{u}))} (-1)^{\tr(e_j(\tilde{u} \cdot h))} \hat{S}_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} \otimes \tau^W_h\\
  1446		&= \sum_{g_W} \sum_a  (-1)^{\tr(e_j (\tilde{u} \cdot\coded(g_W) + a))} \hat{S}_{g_W}^W \otimes \Big( \sum_{h:\, h\cdot \tilde{u} = a}\tau^W_h\Big)\\
  1447			&= \sum_{g_W} \sum_a  (-1)^{\tr(e_j (\tilde{u} \cdot\coded(g_W) + a))} \hat{S}_{g_W}^W \otimes \tau^W_a(\tilde{u})\\
  1448			&= 		\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \;,
  1449		\end{align*}
  1450		where the first equality uses the definition of $\tau^W(e_j \tilde{u})$, the second uses the definition of $\hat{S}^W_{g_W}$ and regroups terms, the third uses the definition~\eqref{eq:def-tauwu} of $\tau^W_a(\tilde{u})$, and the last is by a change of variables. These equations in particular show that the observable $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$ is Hermitian and squares to the identity, because the measurement $\{ \hat{S}_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} \}$ is projective. 
  1451		Furthermore, it can be verified by direct calculation that the observables $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$ satisfy the same relations as the generalized Pauli group. Specifically, for all $j,j' \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$, $\tilde{u}, \tilde{v} \in \F_q^\nqubits$,
  1452		\[
  1453			\tilde{X}^j(\tilde{u}) \tilde{Z}^{j'}(\tilde{v}) = \begin{cases}
  1454			\tilde{Z}^{j'}(\tilde{v}) \tilde{X}^j(\tilde{u})  & \qquad j \neq j' \\
  1455			(-1)^{\tr((e_j \tilde{u}) \cdot (e_j \tilde{v}))} \tilde{Z}^{j}(\tilde{v}) \tilde{X}^j(\tilde{u}) & \qquad j = j'
  1456			\end{cases}~.
  1457		\]
  1458		The next lemma shows that the measurements $\{ \tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a \}$  and observables $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$  are consistent with the original points measurements, and are self-consistent. 
  1459		
  1460	
  1461	
  1462	
  1463	\begin{lemma}
  1464	  \label{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis}
  1465	Let $\delta_S$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}.
  1466	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, all $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^\nqubits$ and $j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$, the measurements $\{ \tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a \}_{a \in \F_q}$ and observables $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$ satisfy the following properties:
  1467	\begin{enumerate}
  1468	\item (\textbf{Consistency with points measurements}) For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, for all $j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$, and on average over uniformly random $u \in \F_q^m$,
  1469		\[
  1470			\Id_{\alice \alice' \alice''} \otimes \tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a \simeq_{\delta_S} M^{(\Point,W),u}_a \otimes \Id_{\bob \bob' \bob''}
  1471		\]
  1472		and
  1473		\[
  1474			\tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a \otimes \Id_{\bob \bob' \bob''} \simeq_{\delta_S} \Id_{\alice \alice' \alice''} \otimes M^{(\Point,W),u}_a \;.
  1475		\]
